opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's because we're still at a stage where the technology isn't a finished product yet. It's more like infrastructure being built. If you look at where embodied intelligence is today, the hardware is getting cheaper and more capable, and the models are improving quickly, but the gap between a demo and something that works reliably in a real home or factory is still very large. The people who can close that gap right now are developers: researchers, engineers, startups who are willing to deal with the rough edges, collect data, debug failures, and iterate.

For an ordinary consumer, a robot that succeeds eighty percent of the time isn't useful. It's frustrating. But for a developer, eighty percent is a starting point. They can see what fails, why it fails, and build on top of it. So it makes sense that the first real "users" are the people who create the next layer.

There's also the data question. Unlike language models, which could learn from the internet, embodied intelligence doesn't have a huge ready-made corpus of physical interaction data. Someone has to generate it, through teleoperation, simulation, world models, or real deployments. Developers are the ones producing that data and the tools around it. In a sense, they're building the flywheel before the flywheel can spin on its own.

So when I say it's primarily for developers right now, I don't mean it will always be that way. I mean we're in the phase where the ecosystem matters more than the end product. Think of early personal computers or early smartphones before the app ecosystem existed. The value came once enough developers had built on the platform. I think embodied intelligence will follow a similar path. First you empower the builders, and then the applications for everyone else follow.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between demos and reliable use in homes or factories, but does not say embodied intelligence is hard to communicate because it is distant from people’s everyday lives.

r002.rationale: It mentions hardware, physical-interaction data, and real deployments, but does not state that assessing usefulness requires access to physical robotic hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because the thing that doesn't exist yet is the use case. When people talk about embodied intelligence today, they usually jump straight to the end picture, a robot in every home doing the laundry. But if you look at what's actually shippable right now, the hardware is still expensive, the models are still brittle outside of a lab, and nobody has a product that a normal consumer would pay for and keep using.

So who is the real customer at this stage? It's the person who wants to build on top of it. The researcher, the startup, the integrator who has a very specific scenario in mind and is willing to tolerate the rough edges. For them, a platform that gives you a decent foundation model, a sensible hardware abstraction, and tooling to collect data and fine-tune, that's already enormously valuable. It saves them a year of plumbing.

I think of it a bit like the early days of large language models. Before ChatGPT, the API was the product, and the people using it were developers trying to figure out what the killer applications were. The consumer moment came after thousands of people had experimented. Embodied intelligence is at that earlier point. We don't yet know which tasks will cross the threshold where the robot is reliable enough and cheap enough that the economics work. Developers are how you find that out.

There's also a data argument. Language models got to ride on the internet. Robots don't have that. Every deployment, every teleoperation session, every failure case in a real kitchen or warehouse is data that nobody else has. If you're building a platform, your best source of that data is a developer ecosystem that puts the system into a hundred different environments you'd never think of yourself.

So it's not that I think consumers are unimportant. It's that if you try to skip the developer phase and sell directly to households today, you end up with a very expensive demo. I'd rather spend the next few years making the stack good enough that a small team can build something real on it. The consumer product falls out of that, it doesn't come first.

r001.rationale: The response says consumer use cases are not yet ready and robots are not part of a normal consumer product, but it does not state that embodied intelligence is difficult to communicate because it is distant from people’s everyday lives.

r002.rationale: The response discusses expensive hardware and real-world deployments, but does not state that assessing embodied intelligence’s usefulness requires access to physical robotic hardware.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes down to the gap between demonstrating a capability and delivering a product that people can reliably use. With embodied intelligence, you have to bring together perception, decision-making, and physical action. Something can work in a controlled setting and still need a lot of engineering before it works consistently in the real world.

So right now, developers are the people best positioned to use these capabilities. They can choose a specific task, integrate the hardware and software, and handle the failures. For an ordinary user, the expectation is much simpler: I ask it to do something, and it works. They shouldn’t have to debug a robot.

That’s why I see it as primarily for developers at this stage. The immediate opportunity is to give them useful tools to build and test applications. As those applications become reliable and easy to use, the audience can expand.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world reliability requires engineering and that ordinary users should not have to debug robots, but it does not attribute the communication difficulty to embodied intelligence being distant from everyday life.

r002.rationale: The response mentions integrating hardware and software, but does not state that assessing usefulness requires access to physical robotic hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s primarily for developers right now because there’s still a large gap between what the technology can demonstrate and what an ordinary user can reliably do with it. A robot might perform a task in a particular setting, but turning that into something useful across different environments requires a lot of integration, testing, and iteration.

Developers are the people who can work with those limitations today. They can build applications, connect the models to hardware, and figure out where the technology actually creates value. So at this stage, the priority is to give them good tools and a platform to experiment with. As those applications become more reliable and easier to use, embodied intelligence can reach a much broader audience.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between demonstrations and reliable use, but does not say that embodied intelligence is difficult to communicate because it is distant from people’s everyday lives.
